:::{#thm-no-joint-density-diagonal}
#### Not every pair of continuous random variables has a joint density

If $X$ is a continuous random variable,
then the pair $(X, X)$ has no [joint density](#def-joint-pdf).

:::

::: proof

Suppose $f$ were a joint density of $(X, X)$,
and let $L = \set{(x, y) : y = x}$ be the diagonal line.
Every outcome $\outcome$ has $X(\outcome) = X(\outcome)$,
so $\set{(X, X) \in L} = \samplespace$.
For each $x$, the function $y \mapsto \1{y = x} f(x, y)$ is $0$ except at the single point $y = x$,
so its integral over $y$ is $0$.
Then:

$$
\ba
1
&= \Pr((X, X) \in L)
&& \text{(} \set{(X, X) \in L} = \samplespace \text{, and } \Pr(\samplespace) = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \iint_L f(x, y)\,dx\,dy
&& \text{(definition of a joint density)} \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \paren{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \1{y = x} f(x, y)\,dy}\,dx
&& \text{(iterate the integral; Tonelli's theorem)} \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} 0\,dx
&& \text{(the inner integrand is 0 except at } y = x \text{)} \\
&= 0
&& \text{(integrate)}
\ea
$$

which is a contradiction.
Tonelli's theorem allows the iterated integral because $f \ge 0$
([Fubini--Tonelli theorem](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-double-integrals.html#thm-fubini-tonelli);
@billingsley1995probability, Theorem 18.3).

:::
